en: The *Biographies of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the Miscellaneous Piṭaka* does not record the names of the translators; it is appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa and Ānanda were at the city of Saṃkāśya in the kingdom of Magadha.
The Tradition of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the Khuddakanikāya:
Having first paid homage to the Buddha, and then paying homage to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, each received these scriptural collections of the compiled Dharma;
having removed the five hindrances, they listened with single-minded attention.
Regarding the teaching of the collected Dharma, as Ānanda has taught: one should together have faith and delight in this wisdom of Ānanda, which is equal to that of the Buddha.
Listen to the compilation of this Dharma as if it were the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
Ānanda transmits the Dharma out of compassion for sentient beings.
Upholding all dharmas as one views the World-Honored One;
The Supreme Guide views Ānanda and others as fields of merit beyond compare.
Had it not been for Ānanda of the Śākya clan entering nirvana, the True Dharma would have perished, along with the Tripiṭaka.
The Buddha rains down all dharmas, out of compassion for devas and humans;
Ānanda receives and upholds them with a vessel that is complete. Entrusted to him with earnest care, Ānanda’s dharma is thus restored;
it shall never leak away, and this is the name of the collected Dharma.
The analytical and other dharmas are like the lion’s roar.
Each and every thing spoken by Ānanda before [the assembly] was excellent for the bhikṣus.
Ānanda stood alone as the Buddha himself praised him, whether it concerned supramundane wisdom or mundane wisdom.

All is known; Ānanda is like the ocean. You all should place your faith in Ānanda and listen to the Dharma he has collected. It shall completely sever all suffering and lead to the worldly illumination of Nirvāṇa.
The earth shook, and the mountains and seas surged and boiled.
Devas and humans wept: "The World-Honored One has appeared too late; why did his nirvana come so soon?
Devas and humans are left orphaned, and the various paths are overgrown and blocked.
Arhats with supernormal powers of far-reaching vision and divine feet all went to Kuśinagara to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
Eighty-four thousand [arhats], having transcended the outflows, are fields of merit unsurpassed and revered by devas and humans. From the land of Jambudvīpa, all the arhats have come;
they gather together there at the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, along with those who are non-returners.

Those who have attained the fruit of the Once-returner, those who have entered the stream and are progressing in training—these groups are each ten times the number of ordinary bhikṣus, numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
Raising their hands, they weep as they walk, crying out, "Where has the World-Honored One gone? We are blind and deaf; the three poisons have not yet been removed."
Sunk within the five realms of existence, who shall pull me out? There are three thousand five hundred bhikṣuṇīs;
among them are those with supernormal powers, those with outflows and those without outflows, Śakra and Brahmā, as well as countless devas, and the Māndārava flower-maidens.
Come quickly, you Four Great Heavenly Kings, each with your own retinues;
bring speedily the sandalwood and pearl necklaces. Together with the gods of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—nine billion eight hundred million in all—come now to Kauśāmbī.
The fearless King Śreṇika had eighty thousand tusked elephants; eighty thousand famous horses all came to Kauśāmbī.
King Candra of Śrāvastī had seventy thousand powerful, intelligent, and famous elephants; they all arrived at Kauśāmbī. So too did King Ajātaśatru.
The valiant one who has faith in the Buddha, With seventy-five thousand elephants, Came weeping to King Pañcāla;
His name was Mingduanzheng (Vimalaprabha). Sixty thousand elephants and horses all went to Kauśāmbī;
His name was Minwangnuan (Karuṇānuvartin); Yugandhara was his close friend.
Fifty thousand from each group all gathered together; the kings of the various western lands of Fragrance and Multitudes,
arrayed in martial gear and wearing four-colored military uniforms, arrived swiftly with hundreds of thousands of followers,
desiring to behold the Buddha’s remains, while the Dragon King wept and wailed.
Pursuing the various kings and the multitude of Vaiśālī, with elephants, horses, and chariots like those of the devas, they came to Kauśāmbī.
An incalculable multitude, including the lay faithful, beheld the Buddha this very day; they shall now behold his parinirvāṇa.
The sentient beings of the world, numbering thirty-six billion, all went to Kuśinagara bringing their funeral requisites.

The area was a hundred *yojanas* square; Kuśinagara was situated in the center, filled with gods and humans until there was not a single empty space on the ground, while the various devas scattered flowers.
They made offerings to the Buddha’s remains, beating celestial drums and playing music, while a rain of various flowers and incense fell.
The kings and their retinues came to the Buddha’s remains; they all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood surrounding him.
The kings wailed and wept, raising their hands in mournful lamentation.
No longer seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly, Ajātaśatru came weeping and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, crying:
"I am a person who has committed the five heinous crimes; to whom shall you entrust me?
The kings surrounded the corpse, scattering jewels over it in abundance, while they all performed various kinds of music.
The bed was smeared with fragrant clay; the corpse was placed in an iron coffin.
It was filled with sesame oil, and the earth shook. All the kings wailed and wept;
the devas shed tears that fell upon the ground. The Heavenly Kings rained down tears, and all everywhere lamented.
Heaps of celestial sandalwood fuel and various wish-fulfilling incenses are piled upon the ground;
for the kings, the fourfold assembly, Mahākāśyapa and the rest, and the monastic community seated there—
this great field of merit, the foremost of Kāśyapa’s followers, is the object of offerings from all sentient beings.
When the Bhikṣuṇī Āryā, the Lord of Devas, and the King of Men each lit their own corpses and ascended the funeral pyre, the devas and humans wailed and cried out, "Alas, what a tragedy!
What shall become of us? For seven days they made offerings, and all the devas received them.
It was divided into eight portions; the ninth was placed in a jar. Each returned to its original place:

the King and the common people [received their shares], the various devas returned above, the eight classes of spirits returned to their eight portions, and the remainder was obtained by the devas, nāgas, and spirits, while the power of Kauśika was gained by humans.
The first was the establishment of the Stūpa of Merit; the second through the eighth were the eight Stūpas.
The ninth was the Jar Stūpa, and the tenth was the Charcoal Stūpa. These arose in Jambudvīpa.
Kāśyapa, the leader of the Saṃgha, departed from Kauśāmbī and traveled to the kingdom of Magadha to assemble the community of monks.
Kāśyapa spoke to the Saṃgha: "O Bhikṣus, do not depart; you must assemble together so that the Dharma may not perish.
In the midst of the open sky, Kāśyapa struck the ghaṇṭā, desiring that the Dharma endure long and triumph over all Māras. Thus Kāśyapa addressed the assembly.
Together with devas and humans, we shall now assemble the Dharma;
To bring peace to all sentient beings, though the Buddha has entered Nirvana, The Four Truths remain, and the Eightfold Path still exists through which Nirvana may be attained.
The Buddhas of the past possessed long lives, and the people were endowed with merit.
The remaining Dharma draws near; before long it shall be exhausted. People today have short lifespans;
this is the seventh appearance of a Buddha. After his parinirvāṇa, will the Dharma endure for long?
Not returning, yet coming again, one sees the Path but has not yet perfected it. Now the true Saṃgha is assembled.
Those who cannot enter [this state]—the divine eye, the power of psychic travel, the six superknowledges, and all arhats who are selfless—I now gather them together.
Upon hearing the sound of the teaching, the assembly immediately gathered from all sides;
there were eighty thousand members, all of whom were free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
Kāśyapa asked: "Brother Aniruddha, look throughout the world of arhats;
who is it that has not come? Aniruddha then surveyed the great trichiliocosm and saw the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where there was a Kaulapata. Aniruddha informed Kāśyapa.
Kauṇḍinya, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and the Arhats free from outflows—though now summoned by Kāśyapa’s command, they do not come. The World-Honored One has entered Nirvāṇa;
what can one seek in this empty world? Kāśyapa thought to himself: "Which bhikṣu could possibly have such power?"
Regarding the compilation of the sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Buddha:
one who has not seen them all cannot collect the meanings of the twelve divisions of the sūtra-dharmas.
Of those spoken by the Buddha, only Ānanda remains; he is a *srotāpanna*, and it is fitting that he should be appointed for this task.
To bring about the state of outflowlessness, the Elder employed skillful means;

observing Ānanda’s mind, he knew there was compassion within him. Since he had attained the Path not long ago, Kāśyapa told him that he could not enter the assembly: "You should not enter; you must now depart."
Ānanda said: "Venerable Elder, what fault have I committed against the Triple Gem? Kāśyapa replied: "Do you wish to know?
You have committed a great fault against the Buddha and the Saṅgha; you sit upon the Buddha’s Dharma."
The lifespan was reduced by a thousand years because you urged the Buddha to establish minor precepts for women.
When the Buddha wished to explain them, why did you not ask about those minor precepts?
What were your thoughts at that time? You treated the precepts with contempt.
The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; whom shall we now ask?
When the Buddha, weary from his journey, craved water while wearing his great robe, you ultimately did not give it to him.
Was this not a transgression? Such instances of fault exceed measure; this was your doing, not something merely spoken with the mouth.
"Therefore, you must depart," Ānanda sighed deeply; overcome with grief, he wept as the Buddha’s skillful means came to an end.
"Upon whom shall we rely? Having said this, he went and sat beneath a tree.
Through his profound resolve, his outflows were exhausted, and the Buddha-dharma flourished thereby.
Countless billions of devas surrounded Ānanda and came to this great assembly where he sat fearlessly like a lion. From afar, Kāśyapa saw them and said to the monks:
"All of you should rise quickly; Ānanda has now arrived with more than eighty thousand followers."
All were stainless, with Kāśyapa as their leader; they stood with palms joined in welcome.
Kāśyapa raised his hand and said, "Welcome, Ānanda!
He then ascended the high seat to attend to the assembly of monks. Truly, Mahā-Ānanda is the eye for all people.
Having finished attending upon the Buddha, Gautama, your merit is perfected. Behold this assembly of monks and behold the host of devas.
The world has long been afflicted by disease; it suffers from three types of suffering and lacks a protector.
The Way leads to Nirvana; let us joyfully share in a heart of compassion.
As he preached the Dharma for the multitude, Ānanda remained silent.
Kāśyapa then invited him to the seat of honor; with a joyful smile, he let out a lion’s roar.
Kāśyapa thought to himself, "Ānanda is able to preach as we have looked toward one another; today he shall deliver and liberate devas and humans."
Kāśyapa raised his voice: "All sentient beings of great destiny who wish to cross over the world, come here!
As the Buddha has taught, Ānanda should now proclaim all the dharmas that eliminate the suffering of sentient beings."
Like scattered flowers, Ānanda shall compile them; he shall distinguish the Three Piṭakas of the Tathāgata’s teachings according to the inclinations of the assembly.
Seated upon a high throne, Ānanda shall further expound them, so that they may be heard throughout the ten directions by devas, nāgas, and spirits.
The fourfold assembly of disciples, upon hearing the command, arrived immediately.
Like a person parched with heat and thirst who longs for water and hastens toward a river to drink from it,
so did the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the four classes of disciples come to Ānanda.
Among them, hearing the Dharma, countless other multitudes advanced in their studies and realized the Path—
becoming *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, and *anāgāmins*. Following the sound [of the teaching],
twenty-one thousand attained the stage of *anāgāmin*, and forty-two thousand became the assembly of *sakṛdāgāmins*.
Eighty-four thousand *srotāpannas*—these who arrived later also desired to hear the Dharma.
All the kings assembled, along with their ministers and military hosts.
Beholding Ānanda’s dignified demeanor, the multitude was filled with joy, and the great assembly sat down in order.
The square was twelve *yojanas* in extent, and Ānanda stood in its center.
Like the full moon with Śakra on his right and Brahmā on his left, they attended upon Ānanda as if the Buddha were still present. Śakra spoke verses of praise, and the devaputras rejoiced.

Beholding the great assembly, Ānanda was free from fear; just as when the Wheel of Dharma was turned and he surrounded the Buddha, he gazed upon Ānanda’s countenance. His majestic appearance was like that of Brahmā;
he then entreated the Tathāgata, saying, "World-Honored One, please preach the Dharma."
Ānanda, it was thus: when Māra heard his name, he also came here, bringing along his wife, children, ministers, and military hosts.
When Pāpīyān beheld these various multitudes with Ānanda in their midst, he was like the radiance of the sun.
Ānanda’s topknot emerges, its appearance like a mountain peak;
upon his neck, the light of the sun shines upon the assembled multitude. Nanda’s topknot emerges;
Kāśyapa’s neck-light and Aniruddha’s penetrating vision survey the great trichiliocosm, as all the kings are present in the assembly.
Together with the assembly of ministers and billions of people, all within this gathering see the great joy;
Ānanda is courageous and valiant, while Pāpīyas is filled with grief and poison, his heart trembling with fear.
Pāpīyas thinks to himself: "A single Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, there are three types of emergence: The power of the Buddha is great;
when Gautama enters nirvana, they claim to have attained liberation. These three attainments are of a vast scope;
upon seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, their hearts are filled with great joy, [saying] "Gautama’s Dharma has declined."
Without any resentment or opposition, one should employ appropriate means.
To extinguish this remnant of the Dharma, the fourfold assembly of disciples and the various kings shall act;
then Māra will issue a command to the General Siṃha, saying: "Quickly assemble the four divisions of the army and utterly destroy this Dharma."
He immediately manifested transformed soldiers— four kinds of generals— who surrounded the great assembly and let out terrifying cries;
they arrested the practitioners and executed the men and women of pure faith,
slaughtered the kings, and tore apart the sites of practice, leaving the entire congregation in shock.
The fourfold assembly thought to themselves: "From where does this sound arise?
Before their doubts were resolved, the kings heard the noise and were all seized with terror.
Seeing the hosts of Māra’s army, each armed and arrayed for battle, Ānanda reflected in his mind: "Who has come to harass us?"
Beholding this host of soldiers, he realized they were Māra; Ānanda then smiled and commanded the King to halt his carriage.
"As for this chaotic multitude, I shall subdue them myself through the power of wisdom;
with the power of my leaves and my advancing strength, I shall reach out my hand and seize Māra."
Three corpses are tied to his throat: the first is a human corpse, the second a dog corpse, and the third a snake corpse.
Swollen and rotting, they are difficult to approach. Māra then spoke these words:
"Kāśyapa, you have been captured! You are an Arhat; how could you be so distressed by a mere man?"
“Kāśyapa, we previously tormented the Buddha to the utmost; yet the World-Honored One never experienced such distress as he does now.

The Buddha replied with compassion: “Clad in the armor of great loving-kindness, I shall ultimately not inflict harm upon any living beings. We have gathered this Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.”
"I wish for you to cause [the Dharma] to flourish for a long time; why have you come here to disturb my assembly?
The Māra then joined his palms and addressed Ānanda, saying, "Please release me at once;
I shall no longer harass people. Ānanda made him take an oath, and Kāśyapa did likewise.
If the assembly were later to be in disorder, the corpse would return with the cangue around its neck; the three corpses would vanish and Pāpīyān would be spared.
Māra would then become sorrowful and terrified, retreating to stand apart on one side.
The devas would acclaim it as virtuous, the Buddha-dharma would achieve victory, and the bequeathed teaching would endure for a long time.
One should always be victorious over Māra; Kāśyapa commands the assembly: "All must be tranquil and composed.
Ānanda now speaks according to what the Buddha has expounded. All the kings arise and wait with palms joined;
all the devas are filled with joy as the Worthy One gazes upon their faces.
Kāśyapa addressed the challenge: "The time has come to preach the sutras; open this precious casket and reveal the supreme Dharma!
What is taught in the *Ekottarika*? What is taught in the *Daśottara*? What is taught in the *Nidāna*?
What is taught in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*? Ānanda laughed heartily.
The Lion yawned and stretched, looked around at the assembly, and said: "Thus have I heard at one time.
At that moment, the earth shook, and ten million devas and humans attained the Dharma-eye.
This is from the *Ekottarika Āgama* of Śrāvastī, titled "The Tenfold Increase."
Explaining the *Madhyamāgama*: "Māra exhausted all realms. Other sūtras likewise expound this in various places.
Ānanda, based on these sūtras, preached them for the great assembly;
he compiled all the sūtras together to form one piṭaka, and the Vinaya as the second piṭaka.

The Great Dharma Tripiṭaka: the Āgamas as the Sūtra Piṭaka; the Great Dharma of the Vinaya and the three divisions of the Abhidharma as the equal and correct [Abhidharma Piṭaka]; thus they constitute the Tripiṭaka.

Having already explained the catalog of the fundamental texts and various distinct teachings, these are now collected together with the diverse miscellaneous works and further formed into a single Piṭaka.
The four divisions of the separate sūtras are called the Āgamas: the Ekottarika, Madhyama, Dīrgha, and Saṃyukta Āgamas;
the Vinaya according to the Dharma; those [rules] for offenses that may arise during long periods of youth;
ascetic practices placed at the end; and the various sections of the Great Dharma.
The Name Arising from Action; First, the Analysis.
Then, the four Āgamas—the Dīrgha, Madhyama, Ekottarika, and Saṃyukta—each increasing by one. Regarding the question posed by Kāśyapa:
"What is the meaning of this? each answer is provided in response to the inquiry. [Finally,] the bhikṣu recollects the Buddha.
Because the mind is thus disciplined, it is called the "Incremental" (Ekottara).
Following this, one contemplates these two dharmas with a virtuous mind, and two further dharmas arise: the stilling of the mind and analytical discernment.
These three bases yield three knowledges: the recollection of past lives and the exhaustion of outflows. These four bases constitute the Four Noble Truths.
The Discourse on the Five Bases and the Five Faculties; the Discourse on the Six Bases and the Six Elements; the Discourse on the Seven Bases and the Seven Factors of Enlightenment;
the Discourse on the Eight Bases and the Eight Right Efforts; the Discourse on the Nine Bases and the Nine Stoppages; the Discourse on the Ten Bases and the Ten Powers;
and the Discourse on the Eleven Bases—these are called the "Discourses on the Cowherd Boy. [They conclude with] the Discourse on Loving-kindness.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* concludes. From this principle, one should explain each item of this scripture individually;
therefore, it is named "Incremental" (*Ekottara*). It is like a painter who delineates forms and colors in distinct sections;
this is the first "one-increment," wherein various [teachings] are compiled and combined.
Just as with medicine that is limitless, being compounded according to the illness,
it is named "the pill of such-and-such"; thus, because each individual thread is woven warp and woof to form cloth,
it is called "the incremental" (*ekottara*) through this successive exposition, just like the blending of various substances.
It is named the "Collection of Sounds of Emptiness," comprising various sūtras; therefore it is called the *Ekottarika*.
Just as grass and wood, with mud and earth, are raised to form a wall that encloses space and thus becomes a house, so too do giving and morality lead to rebirth in heaven and to nirvāṇa.
Because it is surrounded by meanings, it is called "Incremental" (Ekottarika).
Just as a single lump of clay is fashioned into various vessels, so too is this "one-increment":
from this, one should know that various meanings are combined; thus, the various meanings are expounded, and from this sutra they all emerge.
One should uphold the *Ekottarika* [in such a way that] it is neither too long nor too short;
when the meaning is joined so as to form a couplet, it is called the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Furthermore, the characters are neither coarse nor excessively fine, and the words and meanings are perfectly balanced; for these reasons, it is named "Middle."
Having removed the superior and the inferior, one speaks of the Middle Dharma; because it abandons "that" and "self," it is called the *Madhyama-āgama*.
Small evils and great evils, as well as delusion and doubt, are all destroyed through the contemplation of the True Truths;
for this reason it is called "Middle. Within this, there is an extended exposition.
Including those of previous lives, through the cycles of kalpas and worlds;
therefore it is called "Long" (*dīrgha*), for it calculates long-term cessation and the bliss of the heavens—those who hear this rejoice, hence it is named "Long.
It encompasses the Buddhas of the seven past generations as well as the Mahāyāna.

The Nirvāṇa of the Buddha is therefore called "long. Among all treasures, the calculation of many *cakravartin* kings is what the various kings delight to hear; thus it is named "long. This Dharma should be relied upon as the standard;
though one may delight in learning it, there is forgetfulness, yet one desires to sever all fetters.
Therefore it is called "mixed" (*saṃkīrṇa*). These dharmas are equally contained;
because their meanings and flavors are shared and one hears them together, thereby severing doubt, they are named "equally contained" (*saṃgraha*).
This is the destination of the meditative wisdom of the stage of practice; because one equally perceives all dharmas, this is named "equally contained."
Within this entire scripture, the two ends of practice are summarized. Because those who hear it harbor many doubts, it is called the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Collected Scriptures).
It includes miscellaneous scriptures outside the formal divisions and verses of praise by various devas;
thus it is named "Collected" (*saṃyukta*). Those teachings that are closely associated with the Dharma are included therein.
Attaining a well-purified mind and severing all disputes, it is therefore called the precept of discernment within the Vinaya.
Attaining pure diligence, those who hear it are all harmonized;
this is called the Vinaya. When a bhikṣu practices this, he gains benefit therein.
Because it shatters all fetters, it is called the precepts (*śīla*). The bhikṣu who endures the defilements of the fetters trains in this;
it eliminates all evil conduct—this is called the contemplation of the precepts.
By observing all phenomena, one gains benefit from the Dharma and falls upon the ground of the Deathless (*amṛta*).
Therefore it is called Vinaya. Kātyāyana has finished its composition. He presented it to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "This is a supreme teaching;
it shall be named 'The Supreme Teaching' (Uttaradharma). Within it, ignorance is destroyed and benefit is bestowed upon the world.
This clarifies all the various sūtras; therefore, it is called the Great Dharma."
The dhāraṇī that subdues non-Buddhists and cuts off arrogance; the vanguard banner of all dharmas is called the Great Dharma.
It is like a bright lamp that illuminates all things so that their various forms may be seen;
therefore it is named the Great Dharma. This is the meaning of these various sutras.
Like nectar from a thorn, this is the flavor of all dharmas.
Diligently contemplate and uphold the meaning of these great teachings, the various sūtras and vinayas;
do not let them be abandoned or bound within the Tripiṭaka. Discern the meanings of the words, O bhikṣus and devas.
"Excellent! they cried out by the millions. Kāśyapa asked again:
"How may Ānanda speak of the four collections for the sake of sentient beings? Ānanda replied:
"These teachings differ from one another; according to the inclinations and conduct of the various assemblies, these are called the Miscellaneous Collection (Kṣudrakapiṭaka)."

The Buddha spoke of past causes and conditions; the Arhats also spoke of them. Because they include the discourses of devas, Brahmās, and non-Buddhist practitioners, it is called the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka* (Miscellaneous Collection).
It contains many verses and addresses the twelve links of dependent origination through various distinct approaches; this is named the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*. [It comprises] three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
In the life of a Bodhisattva, whatever is born serves as a condition;
therefore, within the Tripiṭaka, there are many accounts of past lives (pūrvayoga) and many accounts of births.
Because this differs from the Āgamas, it is called the Kṣudrakapiṭaka (Miscellaneous Piṭaka). The teachings of the Kṣudrakapiṭaka praise the births of Bodhisattvas.
The various meanings herein are for the most part found within the Tripiṭaka;
they are all combined and the various dharmas are bound together in one place. What kind of bhikṣu would be able to uphold them entirely?
In the future age, bhikṣus will be mostly ignorant; such people as these will not be able to do so.
Having mastered the entirety of the Tripiṭaka, one shall later act as a teacher.
Since verses emerge from the sūtras, they increase accordingly; therefore, they are not [merely] combined.
In various places there are those who delight in the four Āgamas, some who delight in the Vinaya, and others who delight in the Great Dharma.
Some preferred the outer verses (*bāhya-gāthā*), while others preferred the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.

Therefore, not all dharmas were explained under a single name; rather, the four Āgamas were compiled, and the various numerical lists along with the great Dharma of the Vinaya were gathered together to form the Tripiṭaka. Having heard this Dharma, [he]...
Three thousand gods and humans, and eight thousand bhikṣus, have attained the exhaustion of outflows and the state of non-returning;
ten thousand have become once-returners, and countless gods and humans have realized the path of seeing. May this Dharma endure for a long time for the sake of gods and humans.
May all kings be ever victorious and enjoy a full hundred autumns.
May all devas, humans, kings, and bhikṣus alike join in praising this as excellent.
When Ānanda had finished compiling the Dharma as he had spoken it, the devas and humans each returned to their respective places, as did the fourfold assembly of disciples.
They all returned to their respective abodes after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the others were north of the city of Saṃkāśya in the kingdom of Magadha.
The Tripitaka of the authentic scriptures and the Khuddakagantha (Miscellaneous Canon) were compiled;
what is commonly referred to as the "four baskets" is a collective term for these [two] categories.
In total there are two hundred *śloka* verses;
the *Ekottarika Āgama* consists of eleven sections, ranging from one to ten.
He compiled the *Ekādaśa-vastuka-sūtras*,
beginning with the *Gopālaka-ekādaśa-vastuka-sūtra* and concluding with the *Maitrī-caryā-ekādaśa-vastuka-sūtra*.
Following what was cited, this sutra was extracted;
because the matters were interconnected, they were combined into a single fascicle.
This is the *Gopālaka-sūtra*.
The Buddha spoke of eleven matters concerning the tending of cattle to illustrate that a bhikṣu who possesses the eleven practices of the Path becomes like a tree rooted in the Way,
with flourishing branches and leaves that provide abundant shade and shelter.
Because the cowherd boy conceived a thought while at his seat,
the Buddha, knowing his intention, spoke of eleven matters for the sake of one who practices;
the cowherd immediately understood and attained arhatship.
The Tradition of the Compilation of the Tripiṭaka and the Khuddakanikāya (Miscellaneous Piṭaka)
